q: Why are my Klaviyo emails going to the Gmail promotions tab?
a: Gmail sorts mail with promotional content, heavy images and marketing headers into the Promotions tab automatically. That is normal for marketing email and is not the same as spam, so judge your results by engagement rather than tab placement.
detail: Gmail uses signals such as bulk sending, tracking links, image-heavy layouts and sales language to classify mail. Marketing email from an ecommerce brand will usually land in Promotions, and that tab is still read by many shoppers.

Trying to force inbox placement with tricks tends to hurt more than it helps. Focus on sending to engaged subscribers, authenticating your domain and writing messages people want to open, because those habits protect sender reputation in every tab.
If real subscribers say they never see your mail, ask them to drag a message to Primary or reply once. Those actions are positive signals, but they should be a request, never a trick.
example: A skincare brand notices its newsletters appear under Promotions for Gmail users. Instead of redesigning everything as plain text, it checks click and purchase rates for those readers, finds them healthy, and keeps the layout while asking new subscribers to move the welcome email to Primary.

q: How many emails should a winback flow have?
a: Most winback flows work well with two to four emails spread over a few weeks. Stop once someone engages, and move people who still ignore every message into a sunset process rather than continuing to send.
detail: A winback flow targets past customers who have not bought for longer than their usual repeat cycle. The first message can be a soft reminder, the next can show what is new, and a final message may carry an incentive if your margins allow.

More emails is not automatically better, because repeated messages to unengaged people raise unsubscribe and complaint risk. Set the delay by your average time between orders, not by a generic calendar.
Add an exit condition so anyone who orders or clicks leaves the flow immediately, and review results by revenue per recipient.
example: A pet supplies store finds that customers usually reorder food every few weeks. Its winback flow starts only after that window has clearly passed, sends three emails over about two weeks, and exits anyone who places an order at any point.

q: Should I buy an email list for my store?
a: No. Purchased lists contain people who never agreed to hear from you, which causes high complaints, bounces and spam traps, and it breaches the rules of most email providers and many privacy laws.
detail: Consent is the foundation of email marketing. People on a bought list did not choose your brand, so they rarely engage, and they often mark messages as spam.

Even one large send to a bad list can damage sender reputation for months and may get your account suspended by your email platform. Recovering inbox placement takes far longer than any list growth is worth.
Grow the list with consented signups instead: onsite forms, checkout opt-ins, giveaways with clear terms and content people want to receive.
example: A new store is tempted by a seller offering thousands of addresses cheaply. It declines, adds a signup form to its homepage and checkout, and offers a useful size guide in return for an email. The list is smaller but it actually buys.

q: How do I write a good preheader for marketing emails?
a: Write the preheader as a second line of the subject: a short, specific sentence that adds new information rather than repeating it. Set it deliberately, since otherwise inboxes pull in stray text from the email body.
detail: The preheader is the preview text shown beside or beneath the subject line in most inboxes. It is valuable space, so use it to add a benefit, a deadline or a detail the subject left out.
Keep it concise so it is not cut off on phones, and avoid placeholder text such as view in browser. Test how it reads next to the subject on a mobile device.
Some inboxes pad the preview with hidden characters, so check that nothing odd leaks into it.
example: A subject line reads that the new autumn collection has landed. The preheader adds that the three most popular jackets are back in stock in all sizes. Together they tell the reader why to open without repeating each other.

q: How should I handle bounced emails?
a: Remove hard bounces immediately and stop retrying them, and monitor soft bounces for repeats. Most email platforms suppress hard-bounced addresses automatically, so check that this setting is on and review the cause if bounces rise.
detail: A hard bounce means the address is invalid or does not exist, and continuing to send to it signals poor list hygiene to mailbox providers. A soft bounce is temporary, for example a full inbox or server issue.

Treat repeated soft bounces as a hard bounce after a few attempts. If bounces suddenly increase, look at where the addresses came from, since typos at signup and low quality sources are common causes.
Use form validation and consider double opt-in to keep bad addresses out from the start.
example: A store notices a spike in bounces after a giveaway. It finds that many entries had typos in the domain. It adds address validation to the form, confirms the bad addresses are suppressed and the bounce rate returns to normal.

q: How do I measure whether email is truly incremental?
a: Use a holdout test: withhold a randomly chosen group from a campaign or flow and compare their purchases with the group that received it. The difference is the revenue email actually caused.
detail: Attributed revenue counts orders that followed an email click or open, but some of those buyers would have purchased anyway. A holdout compares like with like and isolates the real lift.
Choose the holdout randomly and keep it large enough to see a difference, and run the test long enough to cover a normal buying cycle. Keep conditions identical apart from the email itself.
Even a rough test can reveal which automations are earning their place and which just claim credit for sales that were already going to happen.
example: A store holds back a random slice of its audience from one promotional campaign. After the sales window closes, it compares purchase rates in the two groups. The gap is smaller than the attributed figure, so it reduces discounting on that campaign.

q: When should an ecommerce brand hire an email agency instead of doing it in-house?
a: Hire an agency when email has real revenue potential but you lack the time, strategy or technical skills to build and test it well. Stay in-house when you have a dedicated person with the experience and bandwidth.
detail: Common signals are a platform that is only half set up, no tested flows, inconsistent sending and nobody owning results. An agency brings repeatable processes and experience across many accounts.

In-house work gives you tighter brand control and day-to-day access, but depends on one or two people. Many brands mix both, with an agency handling strategy and build while the team supplies creative.
Whatever you choose, set clear goals, reporting and ownership of the account from the start.
example: A founder is writing every campaign at night and has never built a browse flow. She hires an agency to set up the core flows and a sending plan, then trains a part-time marketer to run weekly campaigns in-house.

q: How do I set up a browse abandonment flow?
a: Trigger it from a viewed-product event for identified visitors who did not add to cart or buy, wait a few hours, then send one or two emails showing the product they looked at. Keep the tone helpful rather than pushy.
detail: Browse abandonment needs the visitor to be identified, for example through a signup or earlier click. Check that your store integration tracks viewed-product events correctly before building.
Add filters so people who already bought, are in a cart flow or recently received this flow are excluded. This avoids overlapping messages.
Lead with the product and a reason to return, such as reviews or key benefits, and keep discounts for later if margins are tight.
example: A furniture store sees that identified visitors often view a sofa without buying. A flow waits several hours, then sends an email with that sofa, fabric options and delivery information. Anyone who adds to cart moves into the cart flow instead.

q: When should a replenishment reminder email be sent?
a: Send it shortly before the customer would usually run out, based on your product usage time and your own repeat purchase data. Start with an estimate, then adjust using how long customers really take to reorder.
detail: Replenishment suits consumables such as coffee, supplements or skincare. Take the typical time a product lasts and set the delay slightly earlier than that.
Check your data for the median gap between first and second orders, and use separate delays for different products or sizes. A one-size delay will be too early for some and late for others.
Make reordering easy with a direct link, and offer a subscription if you have one.
example: A coffee brand sells bags that last about a month for a typical household. Its flow sends a reminder a few days before that point. After reviewing order gaps, it moves large bags to a later reminder than small ones.

q: Why is my email bounce rate high?
a: High bounces usually come from invalid addresses: typos at signup, old inactive contacts, bought or scraped lists, or a poor-quality form source. Clean the list, validate new signups and check where the bad addresses entered.
detail: Look at the pattern. A spike after a giveaway or import points to a source problem, while a slow creep suggests an aging list full of abandoned addresses.
Separate hard bounces, which are permanent, from soft bounces, which are temporary. Persistent soft bounces should be treated as hard.
Keep sending to bounced addresses and mailbox providers read it as careless list management, which can hurt inbox placement for everyone.
example: After importing an old spreadsheet of contacts, a store sees bounces jump on the next campaign. It removes the imported segment, suppresses the failed addresses and sets new signups to be confirmed before they join the list.

q: What is an acceptable spam complaint rate?
a: Keep spam complaints as close to zero as you can. Major mailbox providers expect very low complaint rates, and Google and Yahoo have published thresholds that senders should stay well below.
detail: A complaint happens when a recipient clicks report spam. Even a small number matters because it directly signals to the mailbox provider that people do not want your mail.
Common causes are sending to people who did not opt in, sending too often and making unsubscribing hard to find. Offering a clear unsubscribe link reduces complaints.
Check complaint data in your email platform and in Google Postmaster Tools if you send meaningful volume.
example: A brand sees complaints rise after a heavy sale week. It reduces sends to less engaged segments, makes the unsubscribe link easier to spot and checks complaint figures after each campaign for the next month.

q: How do I check that my email domain is authenticated?
a: Check that SPF, DKIM and DMARC records exist and pass for your sending domain, using your email platform setup page and a free DNS lookup or header test. Send a test to a Gmail account and view the original message to confirm passes.
detail: Your email platform will usually give you the exact DNS records to publish for your sending domain. After adding them, wait for propagation and use the platform verification button.
In Gmail you can open Show original on a test message and look for pass results next to SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Alignment with your visible from domain matters too.
Repeat the check whenever you change platforms or add a new sending tool.
example: A store switches email platforms and publishes the new records. It sends a test to a personal Gmail address, opens the original message view and sees all three checks pass before turning on its flows.

q: How do I build an email marketing strategy for a new store?
a: Start by building consented list growth, then launch the core automations: welcome, cart abandonment and post-purchase. Add a steady weekly campaign rhythm and review results monthly before expanding.
detail: Core flows run in the background and capture the highest-intent moments, so they come before frequent campaigns. Get them live and working first.
Then plan a simple calendar of campaigns mixing product news, education and offers. Segment by engagement and purchase behavior as data grows.
Choose a few metrics you will review regularly, such as revenue per recipient, click rate and unsubscribes, and test one thing at a time.
example: A new home goods store launches a welcome flow, an abandoned cart flow and a post-purchase flow in its first month. It then sends one campaign a week and reviews results at the end of each month to decide what to test.
